steps.name: prompt
steps.text: Write the introduction for our paper on VoxMol, a score-based method that generates 3D molecules by denoising voxel grids. Cover why molecule search is hard, the main molecule representations used by generative models, the limitations of point-cloud diffusion, how our approach works, and our contributions.

steps.name: skeleton_outline
steps.text:
- Finding novel molecules and limits of search-based approaches
- Generative models and molecule representations
- Point-cloud diffusion models and their limitations
- VoxMol: voxelized representation and denoising networks
- Training and walk-jump sampling
- Advantages and contributions

steps.name: detailed_outline
steps.text:
- Motivation
  - finding novel molecules with desired properties: important problem in chemistry, many domains
  - drug discovery: local search (scoring, ranking) around region chosen by prior domain knowledge
  - drug-like molecular space prohibitively large: exponential in molecular size (cite), ~10^{60} (cite)
  - search: some success, but only small portions (billions to trillions molecules), can't propose new molecules conditioned on desiderata
- Generative models (cite)
  - (i) 1D sequences: SMILES (cite), SELFIES (cite), e.g. (cite)
  - (ii) 2D molecular graphs, nodes atoms/substructures, edges bonds, e.g. (cite)
  - (iii) atoms as 3D points
  - 3D arguably most complete: atom types, bonds, conformation
- Point-cloud diffusion
  - molecules as point sets in 3D Euclidean space + diffusion (cite)
  - equivariant GNNs (cite) as denoising network; effective in discriminative tasks
  - limits: (1) number of atoms known beforehand; (2) atom types vs coordinates: categorical vs continuous, treated separately, score undefined on discrete -> workaround; (3) graph nets only nodes/edges -> long-range dependencies hard as atoms grow
  - message-passing limitations (cite); higher-order message passing helps (cite) but costly, limited to third-order (cite); tradeoffs in next section
- VoxMol
  - new score-based 3D molecule generation
  - like one previous work (cite): atoms as continuous Gaussian-like densities, molecules discretized on voxel grids
  - same denoising architectures as computer vision; workhorse of score-based image models (cite); effective, scale well
- Training + sampling
  - train network to denoise noisy voxelized molecules; Gaussian noise (fixed identity covariance, large noise level) per voxel
  - network parametrizes score function of smooth distribution; noise does not displace atoms (unlike diffusion)
  - two steps (cite): walk = Langevin MCMC on noisy grids; jump = denoise to clean molecules
  - walk-jump sampling (cite); used before for 2D natural images (cite), 1D amino acid sequences (cite)
- Advantages + contributions
  - simpler to train, no atom count needed, no separate distributions (continuous/categorical/ordinal for coordinates/atom types/formal charge); "raw" voxelized molecule
  - expressive architecture -> scales to large drug-sized molecules
  - Figure 1 (Figures 8, 9 appendix): samples from two datasets; learns valences, symmetries
  - differs in data representation, noise model, network architecture, generative algorithm
  - slightly worse than SOTA on QM9 (cite); much better on GEOM-drugs (cite)

steps.name: partial_draft
steps.text:
Finding novel molecules with desired properties is an important problem in chemistry, and it has applications in many scientific domains. In drug discovery especially, the standard computational approaches do some kind of local search, by scoring and ranking molecules, around a region of the molecular space that is chosen based on some prior domain knowledge. The space of possible drug-like molecules is prohibitively large: it scales exponentially with the molecular size and is estimated to be around 10^{60}. So searching this space is very hard. Search-based approaches have some successes in practice, but they have severe limitations. We can only explore very small parts of the molecular space (on the order of billions to trillions molecules), and these approaches cannot propose new molecules conditioned on some desiderata.

Generative models for molecules have been proposed to get around these limitations and explore the molecular space more efficiently. These approaches usually use one of these types of molecule representations: (i) one-dimensional sequences such as SMILES or SELFIES (e.g., some works), (ii) two-dimensional molecular graphs, where nodes are atoms or molecular substructures and edges are bonds between them (e.g., some works), or (iii) atoms as three-dimensional points in space. Molecules are entities that lie in three-dimensional space, so 3D representations are arguably the most complete ones, since they contain information about atom types, their bonds and the molecular conformation.

Recent generative models treat molecules as a set of points in 3D Euclidean space and apply diffusion models to them. With point-cloud representations we can use equivariant graph neural networks as the denoising network of the diffusion model, and these networks are known to be very effective in molecular discriminative tasks. But point-based diffusion approaches have some limitations for generative modeling. First, the number of atoms in the molecule (i.e., nodes on the 3D graph) that will be diffused has to be known beforehand. Second, atom types and their coordinates have very different distributions (categorical and continuous variables, respectively) and are treated separately. A score function is undefined on discrete distributions, so some workaround is needed. Finally, graph networks only operate on nodes and edges (single and pairwise iterations, respectively), so capturing long-range dependencies over multiple atoms (nodes) can get difficult as the number of atoms increases. This is related to the limitations of the message-passing formalism in graph neural networks. Higher-order message passing can help with this to a degree, but it comes at a significant computational cost and has been limited to third-order models (see next section for more discussion of the tradeoffs between model expressivity and built-in equivariance).

- VoxMol: new score-based 3D molecule generation
  - like one previous work: atoms as Gaussian-like densities, molecules on voxel grids
  - computer-vision denoising architectures; workhorse of score-based image models; effective, scale with data
- Training + sampling
  - denoise noisy voxelized molecules; Gaussian noise per voxel; score of smooth distribution; atoms not displaced
  - walk (Langevin MCMC) then jump (denoise); walk-jump sampling; used for 2D images, 1D amino acid sequences
- Advantages + contributions
  - simpler, no atom count, no separate distributions; scales to drug-sized molecules
  - Figure 1 (Figures 8, 9 appendix): valences, symmetries
  - slightly worse on QM9, much better on GEOM-drugs

steps.name: rough_draft
steps.text:
Finding novel molecules with desired properties is an important problem in chemistry, and it has applications in many scientific domains. In drug discovery especially, the standard computational approaches do some kind of local search, by scoring and ranking molecules, around a region of the molecular space that is chosen based on some prior domain knowledge. The space of possible drug-like molecules is prohibitively large: it scales exponentially with the molecular size and is estimated to be around 10^{60}. So searching this space is very hard. Search-based approaches have some successes in practice, but they have severe limitations. We can only explore very small parts of the molecular space (on the order of billions to trillions molecules), and these approaches cannot propose new molecules conditioned on some desiderata.

Generative models for molecules have been proposed to get around these limitations and explore the molecular space more efficiently. These approaches usually use one of these types of molecule representations: (i) one-dimensional sequences such as SMILES or SELFIES (e.g., some works), (ii) two-dimensional molecular graphs, where nodes are atoms or molecular substructures and edges are bonds between them (e.g., some works), or (iii) atoms as three-dimensional points in space. Molecules are entities that lie in three-dimensional space, so 3D representations are arguably the most complete ones, since they contain information about atom types, their bonds and the molecular conformation.

Recent generative models treat molecules as a set of points in 3D Euclidean space and apply diffusion models to them. With point-cloud representations we can use equivariant graph neural networks as the denoising network of the diffusion model, and these networks are known to be very effective in molecular discriminative tasks. But point-based diffusion approaches have some limitations for generative modeling. First, the number of atoms in the molecule (i.e., nodes on the 3D graph) that will be diffused has to be known beforehand. Second, atom types and their coordinates have very different distributions (categorical and continuous variables, respectively) and are treated separately. A score function is undefined on discrete distributions, so some workaround is needed. Finally, graph networks only operate on nodes and edges (single and pairwise iterations, respectively), so capturing long-range dependencies over multiple atoms (nodes) can get difficult as the number of atoms increases. This is related to the limitations of the message-passing formalism in graph neural networks. Higher-order message passing can help with this to a degree, but it comes at a significant computational cost and has been limited to third-order models (see next section for more discussion of the tradeoffs between model expressivity and built-in equivariance).

In this work we introduce VoxMol, a new score-based method to generate 3D molecules. Similar to one previous work, and unlike most recent approaches, we represent atoms as continuous (Gaussian-like) densities and molecules as a discretization of 3D space on voxel (i.e., a discrete unit of volume) grids. With voxelized representations we can use the same kind of denoising architectures that are used in computer vision. These neural networks are the workhorse behind the success of score-based generative models on images, e.g. several works, and they are very effective and scale very well with data.

We first train a neural network to denoise noisy voxelized molecules. Noisy samples are made simply by adding Gaussian noise (with a fixed identity covariance matrix scaled by a large noise level) to each voxel in the molecular grid. This denoising network also parametrizes the score function of the smooth/noisy distribution. Unlike diffusion models, the noise process we use here does not displace atoms. Then we use the (learned) denoising network to generate molecules in two steps: (i) (walk) sample noisy density grids from the smooth distribution with Langevin Markov chain Monte Carlo (MCMC), and (ii) (jump) recover "clean" molecules by denoising the noisy grid. This sampling scheme is called walk-jump sampling in the same work, and it has been applied successfully before to 2D natural images and 1D amino acid sequences.

Compared to point-cloud diffusion models, VoxMol is simpler to train, it does not need to know the number of atoms beforehand, and it does not treat features as different distributions (continuous, categorical and ordinal for coordinates, atom types and formal charge). We only use the "raw" voxelized molecule. Also, because of its expressive network architecture, our method scales better to large, drug-sized molecules. Figure 1 (and Figures 8, 9 on appendix) shows voxelized molecules and the corresponding molecular graphs generated by our model, trained on two different datasets. These samples show visually that our model learns valences of atoms and symmetries of molecules.

To sum up the main contributions of this work: We present VoxMol, a new score-based method for 3D molecule generation. It is different from current approaches, which are usually diffusion models on point clouds, in the data representation, the noise model, the network architecture, and the generative modeling algorithm. Our experiments show that VoxMol is slightly worse than state of the art on a small dataset (QM9), but it outperforms it by a large margin on a challenging, more realistic dataset of drug-like molecules (GEOM-drugs).

Voxelized representations allow us to use the same type of denoising architectures used in computer vision. These neural networks, the workhorse behind the success of score-based generative models on images, e.g. [33,34,35], are very effective and scale very well with data.

We start by training a neural network to denoise noisy voxelized molecules. Noisy samples are created simply by adding Gaussian noise (with a fixed identity covariance matrix scaled by a large noise level) to each voxel in the molecular grid. This denoising network also parametrizes the score function of the smooth/noisy distribution. Note that, in contrast to diffusion models, the noise process used here does not displace atoms. We then leverage the (learned) denoising network to generate molecules in two steps [36]: (i) (walk) sample noisy density grids from the smooth distribution via Langevin Markov chain Monte Carlo (MCMC), and (ii) (jump) recover "clean" molecules by denoising the noisy grid. This sampling scheme, referred to as walk-jump sampling in [36], has been successfully applied before to 2D natural images [37,38] and 1D amino acid sequences [39].

Compared to point-cloud diffusion models, VoxMol is simpler to train, does not require knowing the number of atoms beforehand, and does not treat features as different distributions (continuous, categorical and ordinal for coordinates, atom types and formal charge); we only use the "raw" voxelized molecule. Moreover, thanks to its expressive network architecture, our method scales better to large, drug-sized molecules. Figure 1 (and Figures 8, 9 on appendix) illustrates voxelized molecules and the corresponding molecular graphs generated by our model, trained on two different datasets. These samples show visually that our model learns valences of atoms and symmetries of molecules.

The main contributions of this work can be summarized as follows. We present VoxMol, a new score-based method for 3D molecule generation. The proposed method differs from current approaches, usually diffusion models on point clouds, in terms of the data representation, the noise model, the network architecture, and the generative modeling algorithm. We show in experiments that VoxMol performs slightly worse than state of the art on a small dataset (QM9 [40]), while outperforming it by a large margin on a challenging, more realistic drug-like molecules dataset (GEOM-drugs [41]).
